parole.significato: A fact or statement used to support a proposition; a reason.

parole.significato: A tumour or other malignant swelling.

parole.significato: A military document entitling a commissioned officer to hold a higher rank temporarily, but without an increase in pay.

parole.significato: To cause a rowdy disturbance; embroil.

parole.significato: A horn used by hunters.

parole.significato: A callus.
parole.testo: From Middle English callosite, collositee, calosite, from Anglo-Norman calosité (compare Old French chalosité), from Latin callōsitās, equivalent to callous + -ity.

parole.significato: An embankment holding in water; a dam.

parole.significato: One who chafes.

parole.significato: A playing piece in the game of checkers (British: draughts), or certain other table games such as backgammon.

parole.significato: clary sage (Salvia sclarea)

parole.significato: A person who or thing that collects, or which creates or manages a collection.

parole.significato: One who commissions something.

parole.significato: Anything movable (a good) that is bought and sold.

parole.significato: A sexual partner, especially a woman, to whom one is not or cannot be married.

parole.significato: An alliance.

parole.significato: One who confesses faith in Christianity in the face of persecution, but who is not martyred.

parole.significato: One who conserves, preserves or protects something.

parole.significato: A benefactor; someone who donates to charity or some cause.

parole.significato: The act of converting something or someone.

parole.significato: An object forfeited to the state (and supposedly to God) because it had caused the death of a person.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman deodande, from Latin deodandum, from Deo dandum (“to be given to God”).

parole.significato: A lengthy discourse on a subject.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman descaunt, from Medieval Latin discantus. Doublet of discant.

parole.significato: A coin worth one-tenth of a dollar, that is, ten cents.
parole.testo: From Middle English dime, from Anglo-Norman disme (“one tenth, tithe”) (modern French dîme), from Medieval Latin decima, from Latin decima (pars) (“tenth (part)”). Doublet of decim, decima, and decime.

parole.significato: To deforest.
parole.testo: From Middle English disafforeten, from Anglo-Norman disaforester and its probable etymon Latin disafforestō. By surface analysis, dis- + afforest.

parole.significato: The act of falling in drops, or the act of pouring out in drops.
parole.testo: From Middle English distillacioun, from Anglo-Norman distillacioun, from Latin distīllātiōnem, accusative of distīllātiō.

parole.significato: A process of choosing a leader, members of parliament, councillors, or other representatives by popular vote.

parole.significato: The male monarch or ruler of an empire.
parole.testo: From Middle English emperour, from Anglo-Norman emperour, from Latin imperātorem, derived from imperō (“to command”). Doublet of imperator. Displaced earlier Old English casere, from Latin Caesar.

parole.significato: Ensuing; following as a consequence.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ensuant, present participle of ensivre, itself from Latin īnsequor (“to follow, to pursue”).

parole.significato: Whole; complete.
parole.testo: From Middle English entere, enter, borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (“whole”). Doublet of entier and integer.

parole.significato: An office of revenue taxation; a treasury.
parole.testo: From Middle English escheker, from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium. This is because the cloth on which the treasurer counted money was chequered like a chessboard.

parole.significato: A person who carries out some task.
parole.testo: From Middle English executour, from Anglo-Norman executour, from Latin exsecūtor, agent noun of exsequor.

parole.significato: The act of exemplifying; a showing or illustrating by example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplificacion, exemplification, from Anglo-Norman exemplification, from Medieval Latin exemplificātiō.

parole.significato: To change (something) from a smaller form or size to a larger one; to spread out or lay open.
parole.testo: Recorded in Middle English since 1422 (as expanden, expaunden), from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Latin expandō (“to spread out”), itself from ex- (“out, outwards”) + pandō (“to spread”). Doublet of spawn.

parole.significato: To increase in extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre, from Latin extendō (“to stretch out”).

parole.significato: A charlatan or imposter, especially one pretending to be ill, or to tell fortunes.
parole.testo: From Middle English faytour, from Anglo-Norman faitour (cognate with Old French faitor (“doer, maker”), from Latin factor, factōrem, from facere (“do, make”).

parole.significato: Well known.
parole.testo: From Middle English famous, from Anglo-Norman famous, from Latin fāmōsus, equivalent to fame + -ous. Displaced native Old English hlīsful.

parole.significato: A current (constantly changing) trend, favored for frivolous rather than practical, logical, or intellectual reasons.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English facioun, from Anglo-Norman fechoun (compare Jersey Norman faichon), variant of Old French faceon, fazon, façon (“fashion, form, make, outward appearance”), from Latin factiō (“a making”), from faciō (“do, make”); see fact. Doublet of faction.

parole.significato: Fidelity to one's lord or master; the feudal obligation by which the tenant or vassal was bound to be faithful to his l…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English feaute, feute, from Anglo-Norman fëauté, fëuté, from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness”; “homage, fealty” in Medieval Latin), from fidēlis (“faithful”) + -tās (noun suffix); the modern form (for expected *feauty /ˈfjuːti/) is due to learned influence. Equivalent to obsolet

parole.significato: Able to be done in practice.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fesable, from Latin facere, Old French fesable, faisable (“doable”), from fere, faire (“to do”) + -able.

parole.significato: An estate in land in common law in which the land is inherited, but cannot be sold, devised by will, or otherwise alien…
parole.testo: From Middle English fee taille, fetayll, from Anglo-Norman fee tailé, from Medieval Latin foedum talliātum.

parole.significato: Deficient in physical strength.
parole.testo: From Middle English feble, from Anglo-Norman feble (“weak, feeble”) (compare French faible), from Latin flēbilis (“tearful, mournful, lamentable”) by dissimilation, from fleō (“to weep, cry”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-. Doublet of foible.

parole.significato: A receptacle that houses relics of saints.
parole.testo: From Middle English feretory, fertre, feretre, et al., from Anglo-Norman fertre, from Latin feretrum (“bier, funeral litter”), from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron), from the verb φέρω (phérō, “to carry”). Doublet of feretrum.

parole.significato: A colorful, conspicuous structure associated with angiosperms, frequently scented and attracting various insects, and w…
parole.testo: From Middle English flour, from Anglo-Norman flur, from Latin flōrem, accusative of flōs, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to thrive, bloom”). Doublet of fleur, flor, flour, bloom, and blossom. Partly displaced native Old English blostma (which is cognate), whence Modern

parole.significato: To pick out such parts (of a text) as may serve a purpose not intended by the original author; to mutilate; to pervert.
parole.testo: From Middle English garbelen, from Anglo-Norman garbeler (“to sift”), from Medieval Latin garbellare (or a similar Italian word), from Arabic غَرْبَلَ (ḡarbala, “to sift”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Gascon.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Gascoyne, from Anglo-Norman Gascoigne, from Late Latin Wascōnia, from Wascōnēs, modification of Classical Latin Vasconēs (“Basques, Gascons”), from Ancient Greek Οὐάσκωνες (Ouáskōnes). Compare Gascon and Gascony.

parole.significato: Any of the trailing or climbing vines producing fruit with a hard rind or shell, from the genera Lagenaria and Cucurbit…
parole.testo: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of cucurbit.

parole.significato: Animal fat in a melted or soft state.
parole.testo: From Middle English grece, from Anglo-Norman grece, from Vulgar Latin *crassia, noun derived from Latin crassus (“fat, thick”). Doublet of crass.

parole.significato: A viscous water-soluble carbohydrate exudate of certain plants that hardens when it becomes dry, or such a substance as…
parole.testo: From Middle English gomme, gumme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman gome, from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”). Cognate with Spanish goma (“rubber”). Doublet of gumma.

parole.significato: The internal organs of an animal, especially the heart and liver of a pig.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hastelet, from Anglo-Norman hastilet (“roast meat”), diminutive of haste (“spear, spit, roast meat”), from Latin hasta (“spear”).

parole.significato: A thick or heavy-duty cable or rope used to tow or moor a ship.
parole.testo: From Middle English hauser, haucer, from Anglo-Norman haucer, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre (“to raise”), derived from Latin altus (“high”). Altered in English by mistaken association with hawse and perhaps haul. Compare French aussière, haussière.

parole.significato: Someone who inherits, or is designated to inherit, the property of another.
parole.testo: From Middle English heir, from Anglo-Norman eir, heir, from Latin hērēs.

parole.significato: Property which can be inherited.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hereditament, from Anglo-Norman hereditament or its etymon Medieval Latin hērēditāmentum, from Late Latin hērēditō (“to inherit”), from hērēs (“heir”).

parole.significato: Any long-legged, long-necked wading bird of the family Ardeidae.
parole.testo: From Middle English heron, heroun, heiron, from Anglo-Norman heiron, from Medieval Latin hairō, from Frankish and Proto-West Germanic *hraigrō, from Proto-Germanic *haigrô (compare Swedish häger and Danish hejre), dissimilation of *hraigrô (compare Old English hrāgra, Dutch reiger, German Reiher), f

parole.significato: A young sheep of either gender from about 9 to 18 months of age (until it cuts 2 teeth).
parole.testo: From Middle English hogget, from Anglo-Norman hoget and an Anglo-Latin hogettus.

parole.significato: (of a quantity, etc.) To become larger or greater, to greaten.
parole.testo: From Middle English encresen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman encreistre, from Latin increscere (“to increase”), from in (“in, on”) + crescō (“grow”). The noun is from Middle English encres, from the verb.

parole.significato: An official formal accusation for a criminal offence, or the process by which it is brought to a jury.
parole.testo: 18th-century Latinized respelling of Middle English endytement (“action of accusing”), from Anglo-Norman enditement, from enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from Latin indictus.

parole.significato: To wound or cause physical harm to a living creature.
parole.testo: A back-formation from injury, from Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”).

parole.significato: Causing physical harm or injury; harmful, hurtful.
parole.testo: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

parole.significato: Damage to the body of a living thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”). Doublet of injuria.

parole.significato: The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.

parole.significato: A place or institution for the confinement of persons held against their will in lawful custody or detention, especiall…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gayole, borrowed from Anglo-Norman jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Doublet of caveola and related to cage. More at cajole. Fully displaced native Middle English quartern (“prison, jail, cell”), from Old English cwea

parole.significato: An animal, especially a beast of burden.
parole.testo: From Middle English jument, from Anglo-Norman jument or directly from Latin iūmentum.

parole.significato: A group of individuals chosen from the general population to hear and decide a case in a court of law.
parole.testo: From Middle English jure, from Anglo-Norman juree, from Medieval Latin iūrāta, from Latin iūrō (“to swear or take an oath”).

parole.significato: People of a church who are not ordained clergy or clerics.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman laite, from Latin laitas, from Ancient Greek λαός (laós, “people”).

parole.significato: The unlawful taking of personal property as an attempt to deprive the legal owner of it permanently.
parole.testo: Coined in Middle English (as larceni) between 1425 and 1475 from Anglo-Norman larcin (“theft”), from Latin latrocinium (“robbery”), from latro (“robber, mercenary”), from Ancient Greek λάτρον (látron, “pay, hire”). Doublet of latrociny.

parole.significato: A regular court, more specifically a court-leet, in which certain lords had jurisdiction over local disputes, or the ph…
parole.testo: Originated 1400–50 from late Middle English lete (“meeting”), from Anglo-Norman lete and Medieval Latin leta (Anglo-Latin), possibly from Old English ġelǣte (“crossroads”).

parole.significato: metal filings
parole.testo: From Middle English lymail, from Anglo-Norman limaille, from Latin limare, a form of limo (“to file”); see further there.

parole.testo: From letters patents (archaic), from Late Middle English lettres patentes, lettres patent (“document or documents granting a privilege, power, or right, making an appointment or decree, etc.”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman lettres patentes (the plural of lettre patente), from Latin litterae p

parole.significato: To make (something) into a liquid.
parole.testo: From Middle English liquefien, from Anglo-Norman liquefier, from Latin liquefacere.

parole.significato: A liquid, a fluid.
parole.testo: From Middle English licour, from Anglo-Norman licour, from Latin liquor (“fluidity, liquidness, a fluid, a liquid”), from liquere (“to be fluid or liquid”); see liquid. Doublet of liqueur.

parole.significato: Any of the grasshoppers, often polyphenic and usually swarming, in the family Acrididae that are very destructive to cr…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English locuste, locust, from Anglo-Norman locuste, Middle French locuste, and their source, Latin locustam (“locust, crustacean, lobster”, accusative of locusta). parole.significato: An arbitrary tax; in particular, a levy imposed by the English monarch on a certain good beyond ordinary customs duties.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English maltode, from Anglo-Norman maltolt (“unjust tax”), from Medieval Latin malatolta, from mala (“evil”) + tolta (“tax”), the latter from tollīta (“raised”), used in Medieval Latin as past participle of Classical Latin tollō.

parole.significato: A large luxurious house or building, usually built for the wealthy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mansioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mansion, mansiun, from Latin mānsiō (“dwelling, stopping-place”), from the past participle stem of manēre (“stay”). By surface analysis, manse + -ion.

parole.testo: From Middle English marien, from Anglo-Norman marïer, from Latin marītāre (“to wed”), from marītus (“husband, suitor”), from mās (“man, male”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: Material; substance.
parole.testo: From Middle English matere, mater, from Anglo-Norman matere, materie, from Old French materie, matiere, from Latin māteria (“wood”), from māter (“mother”), in which case cognate with Old Armenian մայր (mayr, “cedar”) and մայրի (mayri, “forest”). Doublet of Madeira, mata, mater, matrix, and mother. D

parole.significato: To interfere in or with; to concern oneself with unduly.
parole.testo: From Middle English medlen, from Anglo-Norman medler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin misceō (“to mix”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to work normally performed by a servant.
parole.testo: From Middle English meyneal, from Anglo-Norman mesnal, from maisnee (“household”), from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō (“house”).

parole.significato: A merchant dealing in fabrics and textiles, especially silks and other fine cloths.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman marcer, mercer (“merchant, textile merchant”), from merz (“commodity”) (from Latin merx).

parole.significato: A person who traffics in commodities for profit.
parole.testo: From Middle English marchaunt, from Anglo-Norman marchaunt, from mercans, from the verb mercor (“to trade, deal, sell”).

parole.significato: Relenting; forbearance to cause or allow harm to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English mercy, merci, from Anglo-Norman merci (compare continental Old French merci, mercit), from Latin mercēs (“wages, fee, price”), from merx (“wares, merchandise”). parole.significato: Originally, a plot of land as the site for a dwelling house and its appurtenant interests; now, a dwelling house or res…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English mesuage, messuage (“dwelling house, residence; farmstead; household”), from Anglo-Norman mesuage, messuage (“residence; holding”), probably from Late Latin mesuagium, messuagium, probably ultimately from Latin mānsiō (“abode, dwelling, habitation, home”) or its etymon mānsus

parole.significato: Someone's business or function; an occupation, employment, trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English mister, myster, from Anglo-Norman mester, meister (et al.), from Latin misterium, a medieval conflation of Latin ministerium (“ministry”) with Latin mysterium (“mystery”). Doublet of métier.

parole.significato: The result of mixing two or more substances; a mixture.
parole.testo: A merger of a nominal use of the verb and a borrowing from Anglo-Norman mixte, from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“mix”). Nowadays regarded automatically as the nominal form of the verb.

parole.significato: The crossed iron that supports the upper millstone by resting on the spindle; a millrind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman molin (“mill”), from Late Latin molinum (“mill”), from molere (“to grind”). Doublet of moulin and mill.

parole.significato: Of or relating to death or a funeral; funereal.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortuary, from Anglo-Norman mortuarie (“gift to a parish priest from a deceased parishioner”), from Medieval Latin mortuārium (“receptacle for the dead; mortuary”), neuter form of mortuārius (“of or pertaining to the dead”), from Latin mortuus, perfect passive participle of morio

parole.significato: An animal, usually a horse, used to ride on.
parole.testo: From Middle English mounten, from Anglo-Norman munter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre (“climb”), from Latin montem (“mountain”). Compare modern French monter.

parole.significato: An elevation of land of considerable dimensions rising more or less abruptly, forming a conspicuous figure in the lands…
parole.testo: From Middle English mountayne, mountain, montaigne, from Anglo-Norman muntaine, muntaigne, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem (“mountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *monti (compare Welsh mynydd (“mountain”), Albanian mat (“bank, shore”), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati, “promo

parole.significato: Something secret or unexplainable; an unknown.
parole.testo: From Middle English mysterie, from Anglo-Norman misterie (Old French mistere), from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”). Displaced native Old

parole.significato: A woman born in the state of serfdom; a female serf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman neif m, niefe f (“native, serf”), from Latin nātīvus m, nātīva f (“native”). Doublet of naïf and native.

parole.significato: Worthy of note; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”), from notō (“to note, mark”); in some senses from Middle English note (“benefit, profit, use, advantage”), from Ol

parole.significato: A word that functions as the name of a specific object or set of objects, such as person, animal, place, word, thing, p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English noun, from Anglo-Norman noun, non, nom, from Latin nōmen (“name; noun”). The grammatical sense in Latin was a semantic loan from Koine Greek ὄνομα (ónoma). Doublet of name and nomen.

parole.significato: Quantity of countable things.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English number, nombre, numbre, noumbre, from Anglo-Norman noumbre, Old French nombre, from Latin numerus (“number”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute, to give, to take”). parole.significato: The state of forgetting completely, of being oblivious, unconscious, unaware, as when sleeping, drunk, or dead.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

parole.significato: Someone who orates or delivers an oration.
parole.testo: From Middle English oratour, from Anglo-Norman oratour, from Latin ōrātor.

parole.significato: A bird of prey of genus Pandion that feeds on fish and has white underparts and long, narrow wings each ending in four…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ospray, from Anglo-Norman ospriet, from Medieval Latin avis praedae (“bird of prey”), a generic term apparently confused with this specific bird in Old French on its similarity to ossifrage.

parole.significato: A declaration that an individual cannot benefit from the protection of law in a jurisdiction.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English outlawerie (equivalent to outlawe + -erie), after Anglo-Norman utlagarie /utlarie and Medieval Latin utlagaria, both from Old English utlagu + Latin -aria (suffix that forms abstract nouns from other nouns). By surface analysis, outlaw + -ry.

parole.significato: Complete or partial muscle paralysis of a body part, often accompanied by a loss of feeling and uncontrolled body movem…
parole.testo: From Middle English palesie, from Anglo-Norman paralisie, parleisie et al., from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”), from παρα- (para-, “beside”) + λύω (lúō, “loosen”). Doublet of paralysis.

parole.significato: A (usually) rectangular section of a surface, or of a covering or of a wall, fence etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English panel (“piece of cloth, saddle pad, pane of glass, piece of ice, part, division, jury list, jury members”), from Anglo-Norman panel, panelle (“piece of cloth, saddle cushion”), from Vulgar Latin *pannellus, diminutive of Latin pannus (“cloth, rag, garment”), from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: Any of several species of Parietaria.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English peritorie, from Anglo-Norman paritarie, peritorie, from Late Latin parietāria (“the herb pellitory (noun)”), from parietarius (“of or belonging to a wall (adjective)”), which the modern English form has been remodelled on. Compare pellitory, parietal.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a parish.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parochial and its source Late Latin parochialis, an alteration of paroecialis (“of a church province”), from paroecia, from Hellenistic Greek παροικία (paroikía, “stay in a foreign land”), later “community, diocese”, from Ancient Greek πάροικος (pároikos, “neighbouring, neighbour”)

parole.significato: Land, specifically, an open field, on which livestock is kept for feeding.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pasture, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pastour, from Latin pastūra, from pāscor + -tūra.

parole.significato: An ornate tent.
parole.testo: From Middle English pavilloun, from Anglo-Norman pavilloun, from Latin pāpiliōnem, form of pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”) (due to resemblance of tent to a butterfly’s wings), of unknown origin. parole.significato: Most usually, a very large shield fitted with a stand, like a small moveable wall, carried in front to protect all or m…
parole.testo: From Middle English pavis(e) (paveis, pavas), from Anglo-Norman pavis (compare French pavois), from Latin pavensis, probably from Pavia in Italy. Compare Italian pavese.

parole.significato: The most numerous chess piece, or a similar piece in a similar game. In chess, each side starts with eight; moves are o…
parole.testo: From Middle English pown, from Anglo-Norman poun, paun (“footman”), from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”), derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of peon.

parole.significato: A pagan or heathen, especially a Muslim, or a Jew.
parole.testo: From Middle English paynym, paynyme, from Anglo-Norman paienime, peinime et al., from Late Latin paganismus (“paganism”), from Latin paganus (“pagan”). Doublet of paganism.

parole.significato: To inform on someone; turn informer.
parole.testo: From Middle English pechen, from apechen (“to accuse”) and empechen (“to accuse”), possibly from Anglo-Norman anpecher, from Late Latin impedicō (“entangle”). See impeach.

parole.significato: A stake.
parole.testo: From Middle English peel, pele, from Anglo-Norman pel (compare modern French pieu), from Latin pālus (“stake”). Doublet of pole and pale.

parole.significato: Dangling, drooping, hanging down or suspended.
parole.testo: From Middle English pendaunt, Anglo-Norman pendaunt, pendant, respelled to reflect Latin pendēns, pendentis, present participle of pendere (“to hang, to be suspended”). Compare pendant, which retained the spelling.

parole.significato: Mentha pulegium, a plant of the mint family, formerly much used in various medicinal treatments and as a flea repellent.
parole.testo: Apparently an alteration (after penny) of Anglo-Norman puliol royal, from Latin pūlegium.

parole.significato: A structure or annexe (especially one with a sloping roof) extending from the side of a building, sometimes as protecti…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pentiz (“pentice”), from apendiz (“appentice”), ultimately from a suffixed form of Latin appendō (“to append”). Altered by folk etymology to appear to be a compound of house. Doublet of appentice and pentice.

parole.significato: A survey, a tour; an instance of walking around.
parole.testo: From Middle English perambulacioun, from Anglo-Norman and Latin. By surface analysis, perambulate + -ation, or, by surface analysis, per- + ambulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Precluding debate or expostulation; not admitting of question or appeal.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).

parole.significato: The deliberate giving of false or misleading testimony under oath.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre. Displaced native Old English mānāþ (literally “false oath”).

parole.significato: An individual who has been granted personhood; usually a human being.
parole.testo: From Middle English persoun, personne et al., from Anglo-Norman parsone, persoun et al. (Old French persone (“human being”), French personne), and its source Latin persōna (“mask used by actor; role, part, character”), perhaps a loanword from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu, “mask”). parole.significato: A wasting illness of the lungs, such as asthma or tuberculosis; consumption; phthisis.
parole.testo: From Middle English tisike, from Anglo-Norman, from Latin phthisicus (“suffering from tuberculosis”), from Ancient Greek φθισικός (phthisikós, “consumptive”), from φθίσις (phthísis, “tuberculosis, consumption”).

parole.significato: Hair, especially when very fine or short; the fine underfur of certain animals. (Formerly countable, now treated as a c…
parole.testo: From Middle English pile, partly from Anglo-Norman pil (a variant of peil, poil (“hair”)) and partly from its source, Latin pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pilus.

parole.significato: A flat fold; a doubling, as of cloth; a pleat.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ (plestí) and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced. Doublet of plight (“plait, fold”) and pleat.

parole.significato: A tool for smoothing wood by removing thin layers from the surface.
parole.testo: From Middle English plane, plaine, from Anglo-Norman plaine, from Late Latin plāna (“planing tool”).

parole.significato: Precious metal, especially silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English, partly from Anglo-Norman plate (“plate, bullion”) and partly from Latin plata (“silver”), from Vulgar Latin *platta (“metal plate”), from feminine of Latin *plattus (“flat”).

parole.significato: Any of various wading birds of the subfamily Charadriinae.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English plover, from Anglo-Norman plover, plovier, from Medieval Latin plovarius, pluviārius, of disputed origin; perhaps from Latin pluvia (“rain”).

parole.significato: To adorn, cover, or furnish with feathers or plumes, or as if with feathers or plumes.
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“to adorn, cover, or furnish with feathers or plumes”) is derived from Anglo-Norman plumer (“to cover with or provide with feathers”), or its etymon Latin plūmāre, the present active infinitive of plūmō (“to grow feathers, to fledge; to cover with feathers, to feather; to embroider with a f

parole.significato: Sharp-pointed; keen.
parole.testo: From Middle English poynaunt, poynant, borrowed from Anglo-Norman puignant, poynaunt etc., present participle of poindre (“to prick”), from Latin pungō (“prick”). Doublet of pungent.

parole.significato: Any of many ferns of the genus Polypodium, especially common polypody.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman polypodie, from Late Latin polypodium, q.v.

parole.significato: A writ in law used by the superior courts to remove cases from inferior courts.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pone, from Anglo-Norman pone, from Late Latin pone, from Latin pōne, imperative of pōnere (“to place”).

parole.significato: A quilted military doublet or gambeson worn in the 14th and 15th centuries.
parole.testo: From Middle English purpoynt, from Anglo-Norman purpoint, alteration of perpoint, from Late Latin perpunctum, from per- + punctum (“pierced”). The modern spelling is influenced by French pourpoint.

parole.significato: A proclamation, announcement or preaching.
parole.testo: From Middle English predicacion, from Anglo-Norman predicaciun, from Latin praedicātiō, from praedicō.

parole.significato: To be in the habit of choosing something rather than something else; to favor; to like better.
parole.testo: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō. Displaced native Old English foresettan and foreberan. Doublet of prelate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.

parole.significato: A clairvoyant or clairaudient experience, such as a dream, which resonates with some event in the future.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1533. From Anglo-Norman premunition, from Ecclesiastical Latin praemonitiōnem (“a forewarning”), form of praemonitiō, from Latin praemonitus, past participle of praemoneō, from prae (“before”) (English pre-) + moneō (“to warn”) (from which English monitor). parole.significato: A right, especially when due to one's position or role.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).

parole.significato: To be so presumptuous as (to do something) without proper authority or permission [with to (+ infinitive)].
parole.testo: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).

parole.significato: To speak or behave so as to give a false or simulated appearance.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”), from prae- (“pre-”) + tendō (“stretch”); see tend.

parole.significato: First in time, initial, early.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman primer (“first”), from Latin prīmārius (“first”).

parole.significato: A (male) ruler, a sovereign; a king, monarch.
parole.testo: From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) + capiō (“seize, take”). parole.significato: An outhouse: an outbuilding used for urination and defecation.
parole.testo: From privy (“outhouse”) to clarify the intended sense, likely under the influence of Anglo-Norman privé hostel (attested in an 1139 British source) and Latin domus privata (1141).

parole.significato: The office of a procurator.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procuracie, from Anglo-Norman procuracie, from Latin prōcūrātia, analyzed as procure + -cy (“office of”). Doublet of proxy.

parole.significato: A tax collector.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procuratour, from Anglo-Norman procuratour, from Latin prōcūrātor, from prōcūrō (“to procure”) (English procure). Equivalent to procure + -ator and a doublet of proctor and procurer.

parole.significato: The most senior rank for an academic at a university or similar institution.
parole.testo: From Middle English professor, professour, from Anglo-Norman proffessur and its etymon Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”), from the past participle stem of profiteor (“profess”). By surface analysis, profess + -or.

parole.significato: Suitable.
parole.testo: From Middle English propre, from Anglo-Norman proper, propre, Old French propre (French: propre), from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: Someone who speaks by divine inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophete, from Anglo-Norman prophete, from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”). Displaced native Old English wītga.

parole.significato: Someone who protects or guards, by assignment or on their own initiative.
parole.testo: From Middle English protectour, from Anglo-Norman protectour, protector and its etymon Latin prōtēctor, from prōtegō (“shield, protect”). By surface analysis, protect + -or. Displaced native Old English sċildend.

parole.significato: Used as a proxy or acting as a proxy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procucie, contraction of procuracie, from Anglo-Norman procuracie, from Medieval Latin procuratia, from Latin prōcūrātiō, from Latin prōcūrō (“to manage, administer”) (English procure). Compare proctor.

parole.significato: A learner at a school under the supervision of a teacher.
parole.testo: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).

parole.significato: In words borrowed through Anglo-Norman: involving forward movement or completeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English pur-, from Anglo-Norman pur- (compare modern French pour), from Latin prō- (“forward direction, forward movement”). Doublet of pro-.

parole.significato: The acquisition of title to, or property in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.
parole.testo: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”). Compare Old French porchacier (“to follow, to chase”), which has given French pourchasser (“to chase without relent”).

parole.significato: The process or act of purging, such as by the use of a purgative.
parole.testo: From Middle English purgacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman purgacion, itself borrowed from Latin pūrgātiō; equivalent to purge + -ation.

parole.significato: To convey, imply, or profess (often falsely or inaccurately).
parole.testo: From Middle English purporten, from Anglo-Norman purporter and Old French porporter (“convey, contain, carry”), from pur-, from Latin pro (“forth”) + Old French porter (“carry”), from Latin portō (“carry”).

parole.significato: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.
parole.testo: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.

parole.significato: Any of various small game birds of the genera Coturnix, Anurophasis or Perdicula in the Old World family Phasianidae or…
parole.testo: From Middle English quayle, quaile, quaille, from Anglo-Norman quaille, from Late Latin quaccola (“quail”). (prostitute): So called because the quail was thought to be a very amorous bird.

parole.significato: A part of the entrails of a hunted animal, given to the hounds as a reward.

parole.significato: A fourth part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English quarter, from Anglo-Norman quarter, from Latin quartarius, from quartus. Compare Spanish cuarto (“room, quarters; quarter”). Doublet of quartier.

parole.significato: Released from obligation, penalty, etc; free, clear, or rid.
parole.testo: From Middle English quiten, quyten, from Anglo-Norman quitter, Old French quitter, from quitte (“acquitted, quit”), ultimately from Latin quietus, which itself derives from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁-ti-s, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”). parole.significato: To the greatest extent or degree; completely, entirely.
parole.testo: A development of quit, influence by Anglo-Norman quite. Doublet of coy, quit, quiet, and quietus. For an analogous semantic development from the same root, compare Armenian շատ (šat).

parole.significato: A select body of (usually eminent) justices of the peace, every member of which had to be present to constitute a decid…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English quorum (c. 1426), from Anglo-Norman quorum, clipped from the Anglo-Latin wording of commissions in which certain persons were specially designated as members of a body by the words quorum vos unum esse volumus ad etc. (“of whom we want you to be one assigned to etc.”).

parole.significato: Violent uncontrolled anger.
parole.testo: From Middle English rage, from Anglo-Norman rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs (“anger, fury”). Doublet of rabies. parole.significato: A dried grape.
parole.testo: From Middle English raysyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman reysin (“grape, raisin”), from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Possibly a distant cognate of Persian رز (raz, “vine”). Doublet of raceme.

parole.significato: Being behind, or in the hindmost part; hindmost.
parole.testo: From Middle English rere, from Anglo-Norman rere, ultimately from Latin retro. Compare arrear. Doublet of retro.

parole.significato: An act of recommending.
parole.testo: From Middle English recommendacioun, from Anglo-Norman recomendacion, from Medieval Latin recommendatio. By surface analysis, recommend + -ation.

parole.significato: To heal (an organ or part of the body).
parole.testo: From Middle English rectifien, from Anglo-Norman rectifiier, rectefier (“to make straight”), from Medieval Latin rēctificō (“to make right”), from Latin rēctus (“straight”).

parole.significato: To recompense or reward.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman reguerdoner (“to reward”), from re- + guerdoner (“to guerdon”), from Medieval Latin widerdōnum, alteration of widerlōnum, from West Germanic (whence Old High German widarlōn, Old English wiþerlēan), literally ‘back-payment’, with the second element assimilated to Latin dōnum (“gift

parole.significato: A strap or rope attached to a bridle or bit, used to control a horse, other animal or young child.
parole.testo: From Middle English rein, reyne, from Anglo-Norman reyne, resne, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Classical Latin retineō (“hold back”), from re- + teneō (“keep, hold”). parole.significato: To give in or be swayed; to become less hard, harsh, or cruel; to show clemency.
parole.testo: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526. The noun is from the verb.

parole.significato: A small portion remaining of a larger thing or group; part of a former whole.
parole.testo: From Middle English, contraction of remenant, from Anglo-Norman remanant, present participle of remaindre, from Latin remaneō.

parole.significato: A right to receive rent where the tenant's goods cannot be seized as security for the payment of rent.
parole.testo: From late Middle English rent sek, from Anglo-Norman rente sec; sec rente (literally “dry rent”), ultimately from Latin siccus. Compare Middle English secce (“dry”).

parole.significato: To relate details of (an event or incident); to recount, describe (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.

parole.significato: Dwelling, or having an abode, in a place for a continued length of time; residing on one's own estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English resident, from Anglo-Norman resident, from Latin residēns, present participle of resideō (“to remain behind, reside, dwell”), equivalent to reside + -ent, from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“to sit”). parole.significato: A retardation; a delay.
parole.testo: From Middle English retarden, from Anglo-Norman retarder, from Latin retardō (“to retard”, from re- + tardus (“slow”)).

parole.significato: Thin or watery discharge of mucus or serum, especially from the eyes or nose, formerly thought to cause disease.
parole.testo: From Middle English reume, rewme, from Anglo-Norman reume, from Late Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, humour”). Doublet of stream.

parole.testo: From Middle English rubarbe, from Anglo-Norman reubarbe (modern French rhubarbe), from Late Latin reubarbarum, rheubarbarum, rubarbera, rybarba, probably from Koine Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν (rhêon barbarikón), from ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) + Ancient Greek βαρβαρικόν (barbarikón), neuter of βαρβαρικός (b

parole.significato: To steal from, especially using force or violence.
parole.testo: From Middle English robben, from Anglo-Norman robber, from Late Latin raubāre, from Frankish *raubōn (compare Dutch roven) and Old High German roubōn, raubōn (“to rob, steal, plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *raubōną. Doublet of reave.

parole.significato: A room in a church where sacred vessels, books, vestments, etc. are kept. Sometimes also used by clergy to prepare for…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman sacrestie, from Medieval Latin sacristia.

parole.significato: A long, slender, chiefly terrestrial amphibian of the order Caudata, superficially resembling a lizard.
parole.testo: From Middle English salamandre, from Anglo-Norman salamandre, from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα (salamándra), of uncertain origin (per Beekes, likely Pre-Greek); possibly of Iranian origin, see Persian سمندر (samandar) for more information.

parole.significato: To squeeze (something) tightly into in a rolled or sausage-like form.
parole.testo: From late Middle English sawsiche, from Anglo-Norman sausiche (compare Norman saûciche), from Late Latin salsīcia (compare Sicilian sausizza, Spanish salchicha, Italian salsiccia), feminine of salsīcius (“seasoned with salt”), derivative of Latin salsus (“salted”), from sal (“salt”). parole.significato: A spring onion, Allium fistulosum.
parole.testo: From Middle English scaloun (“shallot”), from Anglo-Norman scalun (variant of Old French eschaloigne), from a Proto-Romance derivation of Vulgar Latin *escalonia, from Latin Ascalonius (in caepa (“onion”) Ascalonius, "shallot"), from Ascalo (“Ascalon”), from Ancient Greek Ἀσκάλων (Askálōn, “Ascalon,

parole.significato: A surface cut or abrasion.
parole.testo: From Middle English scocchen (“to cut”), perhaps from Anglo-Norman escocher (“to notch”), from es- (“intensive prefix”) (from Latin ex-) + Old French coche (“notch”). Not related to Scotch.

parole.significato: A small room, next to a kitchen, where washing up and other domestic chores are done.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English squylerie, from Anglo-Norman squillerie (“office of the servant in charge of plates”), from escuele (“bowl, dish”), from Latin scutella.

parole.significato: To beat or whip; to drub.
parole.testo: From Middle English *scucchen, from Anglo-Norman escucher, from Vulgar Latin *excuticāre.

parole.significato: A stamp used to impress a design on a soft substance such as wax.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sel, sele, from Anglo-Norman seel, from Latin sigillum, a diminutive of signum (“sign”). Doublet of sigil and sigillum.

parole.significato: A sieve; a strainer.
parole.testo: From Middle English sarse, probably from Anglo-Norman cerche, *cerce, from Late Latin *circa. parole.significato: An attempt to find something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English serchen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sercher, Old French cerchier, from Late Latin circō, ,circāre (“to circle; go around; search for”), from circus. Unrelated to German suchen, which is cognate with English seek.

parole.significato: An agent or drug that sedates, having a calming or soothing effect, or inducing sleep.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sedatif, from Anglo-Norman sedatif, from Medieval Latin sēdātīvus, which itself likely influenced the modern spelling. By surface analysis, sedate + -ive.

parole.significato: The role, rank or office of a sergeant; sergeantship.
parole.testo: From Middle English sergeancie, from Anglo-Norman serjancie and Medieval Latin serjantia, sergantia. Compare sergeanty.

parole.significato: Separate, distinct; particular.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman several, from Medieval Latin sēparālis, from Latin sēpar (“separate”). By surface analysis, sever + -al. Not related to severe or seven.

parole.significato: The place where anything is fixed; situation; local position
parole.testo: From Middle English site, from Anglo-Norman site, from Latin situs (“position, place, site”), from sinere (“to put, lay, set down, usually let, suffer, permit”). Doublet of sitio and situs.

parole.significato: An artificial passage for water, fitted with a valve or gate, for example in a canal lock or a mill stream, for stoppin…
parole.testo: From Middle English sluse, alteration of scluse, from Anglo-Norman escluse (“sluice, floodgate”), from Late Latin exclusa (“extrusion, gate”), from Latin exclūsus, form of exclūdō (“to shut out, to exclude”) (English exclude). Cognate to Dutch sluis.

parole.significato: A mixture of mineral particles and organic material, used to support plant growth.
parole.testo: From Middle English soile, soyle, sule (“ground, earth”), partly from Anglo-Norman soyl (“bottom, ground, pavement”), from Latin solium (“seat, chair; throne”), mistaken for Latin solum (“ground, foundation, earth, sole of the foot”); and partly from Old English sol (“mud, mire, wet sand”), from Pro

parole.significato: A piece of plate armour that protects one's shoulder, generally covering less than the pauldron which developed later.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle English spaulde (“shoulder”), from Anglo-Norman espalde, Old French espaule (ultimately from Latin spatula), + English -er. However, compare spallière, ultimately from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: A perfumed ointment, extracted from the plant Nardostachys jatamansi that belongs to the Valerian family and grows in t…
parole.testo: From Middle English spikenard, spikenarde, from Anglo-Norman spicanarde, from Medieval Latin spīca nardī, from Latin spica (“spike”) + nardi (“nard”). Equivalent to spike + nard.

parole.significato: Great light, luster or brilliance.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman splendur, splendour, or directly from its source Latin splendor, from the verb splendeō (“to shine”).

parole.significato: A building, wing or dependency set apart and adapted for lodging and feeding (and training) ungulates, especially horse…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English stable, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stable, from Latin stab(u)lum. From Middle English stable, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stable, from Latin stab(u)lum.

parole.significato: A stopping place.
parole.testo: From Middle English stacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman estation, from Latin statiōnem, accusative of statiō (“standing, post, job, position”), whence also Italian stazione. Doublet of stagione. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἵστημι (hístēmi), στάσις (stásis), Old English standan (whence English stand)

parole.significato: To keep (something) while not in use, generally in a place meant for that purpose.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English store, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stor, from Latin īnstaurāre, from īnstaurō + -āre.

parole.significato: A person or thing that immediately follows another in holding an office or title.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman successour, from Latin successor.

parole.significato: Endurance, especially patiently, of pain or adversity.
parole.testo: From Middle English sufferaunce, from Anglo-Norman suffraunce, from Late Latin sufferentia. By surface analysis, suffer + -ance.

parole.significato: Something suggested (with subsequent adposition being for)
parole.testo: From Middle English suggestion, from Anglo-Norman suggestioun, sugestiun, from Latin suggestiō, from suggerō (“suggest”, verb), from Latin sub- (“from below, up”) + gerō (“to bring”). Equivalent to suggest + -ion. Related to English up-, cast.

parole.significato: One who pursues someone, especially a woman, for a romantic relationship or marriage; a wooer; one who falls in love wi…
parole.testo: From Middle English sutour, from Anglo-Norman suytour, seuter, from Late Latin secutor (“follower, pursuer”).

parole.significato: Something that is supposed; an assumption made to account for known facts, conjecture.
parole.testo: From Middle English supposicioun, from Anglo-Norman supposicion, from Latin suppositiō, suppositiōnem (“supposition”), from sub- (“under”) + positiō, positiōnem (“position; theme”), from positus (“position”), from the perfect passive participle of pōnō, pōnere (“put, place”).

parole.significato: A medicine in the form of a small plug that is inserted into a bodily cavity, especially the rectum, vagina or urethra,…
parole.testo: From Middle English suppositorie, from Anglo-Norman, from Medieval Latin suppositōrium, from Late Latin, neuter of suppositōrius (“placed beneath”), from Latin suppōnō (“to put under”).

parole.significato: One who performs surgery; a doctor who performs operations on people or animals.

parole.significato: To impose and collect a tax from (a person or company).
parole.testo: From Middle English taxen, from Anglo-Norman taxer (“to impose a tax”), from Latin taxāre (“to handle, to censure, to appraise, to compute”).

parole.significato: The act of imposing taxes and the fact of being taxed.
parole.testo: From Middle English taxacioun, from Anglo-Norman taxacion, from Latin taxātio (“rating, appraisal”). By surface analysis, tax + -ation.

parole.significato: Habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions; restrained or moderate indulgenc…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman temperance, from Latin temperantia (“moderation, sobriety, discretion, self-control”), from temperans, present participle of temperare (“to moderate”). See temper. English equivalent temper + -ance.

parole.significato: Pertaining to earth or the material world; earthly, terrestrial (as opposed to heavenly or marine).
parole.testo: From Middle English terrene, from Anglo-Norman terriene, feminine of terrien, from Latin terrēnus, from terra (“earth”).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to a will or testament
parole.testo: From Middle English testamentarie, from Anglo-Norman testamentarie and Latin testāmentārius (“of or belonging to wills”).

parole.significato: The stock; a beam on a crossbow carved to fit the arrow, or the point of balance in a longbow.
parole.testo: From Middle English teler, from Anglo-Norman telier (“beam used in weaving”), from Medieval Latin telarium, from Latin tēla (“web”).

parole.testo: From Middle English tytle, titel, titele, from Anglo-Norman titil, titule and Medieval Latin titulus (“small stroke, diacritical mark, accent”), from Latin titulus (“title”). Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, title, titlo, and titulus.

parole.significato: To (cause to) be in a trance; to entrance.
parole.testo: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

parole.significato: Someone who transgresses.
parole.testo: From Middle English transgressour, from Anglo-Norman transgressour, from Latin transgressor. Equivalent to transgress + -or.

parole.significato: Senses relating to the change of information, etc., from one form to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English translaten (“to transport, translate, transform”), from Anglo-Norman translater, from Latin trānslātus, perfect passive participle of trānsferō (“to transport, carry across, translate”). parole.testo: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”). Equivalent to translate + -ion. Displaced native Old English wending.

parole.significato: An ornamental covering or harness for a horse; caparison.
parole.testo: From Middle English trappyng, trappynge, from trap, trappe (“personal belongings, owndom, household goods”) (compare Middle English trappen (“to deck, caparison”)), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A hidden treasure, subsequently discovered.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tresor trové (“found treasure”), calque of Latin thesaurus inventus, where the past participle trové was interpreted in English as a noun. Perhaps related to trophy.

parole.significato: To roll or move upon truckles, or casters; to trundle.
parole.testo: From Middle English trokel, trocle, trookyl, from Anglo-Norman trocle, from Medieval Latin trochlea (“a block, sheaf containing one or more pulleys”); or from a diminutive of truck (“wheel”), formed with -le, equivalent to truck + -le.

parole.significato: Synonym of Turkey red (“a vibrant red dye or its color”).
parole.testo: From Middle English Turkye, from Anglo-Norman Turkye, Medieval Latin Turcia, from Turcus (“Turk”), from Byzantine Greek Τοῦρκος (Toûrkos), from Classical Persian تُرْک (turk), from Middle Persian [script needed] (twlk' /⁠turk⁠/), from Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰜 (t²ẅr²ẅk²). parole.significato: A change of direction or orientation.
parole.testo: Partly from Anglo-Norman *torn, from Latin tornus, from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos), and partly an action noun from the verb turn.

parole.significato: The flesh of a calf (i.e. a young bovine) used for food.
parole.testo: From Middle English veel, from Anglo-Norman veel, from Latin vitellus, diminutive of vitulus (“calf”). Doublet of vitellus.

parole.significato: A person or a company that vends or sells.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman vendor (Old French vendeor), from Latin venditor (“seller”), from vendere (“to sell, cry up for sale, praise”), contraction of venundare, venumdare, also, as originally, two words venum dare (“to sell”), from venum (“sale, price”) + dare (“to give”).

parole.significato: The meat of a deer, especially one that was hunted in its own natural habitat.
parole.testo: From Middle English venisoun, venesoun, from Anglo-Norman veneisun, venesoun, venesun (“meat of large game, particularly deer or boar; hunt”), from Latin vēnātiō, vēnātiōnem (“hunt; meat from a hunt”), formed on vēnātus, perfect participle of vēnor (“to hunt”). Doublet of venatio and venation.

parole.significato: Violent, destructive and cruel.

parole.significato: A feudal tenant, a serf.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vilein, variant of vilain; from Medieval Latin villanus (“field hand”), from Latin villa (“country home”). Doublet of villain.

parole.significato: Any plant whose stem requires support and which climbs by tendrils or twining.
parole.testo: From Middle English vyne, from Anglo-Norman vigne, from Vulgar Latin vīnia, from Latin vīnea (“vines in a vineyard”), from vīneus (“related to wine”), from vīnum (“wine”), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom (“vine, wine”), from *weh₁y- (“to twist, wrap”). Doublet of wine.

parole.significato: Full of virtue; having excellent moral character.
parole.testo: From Middle English vertuous, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertuous, vertous, ultimately from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. By surface analysis, virtue + -ous. Doublet of virtuoso and piecewise doublet of virtùous.

parole.significato: Countenance; one's face.
parole.testo: From Middle English visage, from Anglo-Norman visage, from Vulgar Latin *vīsāticum, derived from Latin vīsus (“appearance, sight”), derived from vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision. See -age (“noun suffix”).

parole.significato: A member of the peerage, above a baron but below a count or earl.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman viscounte, from Medieval Latin vicecomes, from Latin vice + comes. Equivalent to vice- + count. Doublet of vicecomes and vicomte.
